sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- web_enable: If tools for web search, source checking, content fetching, stored-result retrieval are not already available, call web_enable first whenever current, external, or linked information could help; the tools appear on the next model request.

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

---
name: grilling
description: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea. Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
---

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

name: domain-modeling
description: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when discussing codebase terminology, writing or editing a GLOSSARY.md, or recording or editing an ADR.
---

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── GLOSSARY.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update GLOSSARY.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

# Issue tracker: GitHub

Issues and specs for this repo live as GitHub issues. Use the `gh` CLI for all operations.

## Conventions

- **Create an issue**: `gh issue create --title "..." --body "..."`. Use a heredoc for multi-line bodies.
- **Read an issue**: `gh issue view <number> --json number,title,body,labels,comments`.
- **List issues**: `gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments` with appropriate label and state filters.
- **Make an issue a sub-issue of a parent**: use GitHub sub-issues where available; otherwise put `Part of #<parent>` at the top of the child body.
- **Comment**: `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`
- **Apply/remove labels**: `gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..."` / `--remove-label "..."`
- **Close**: `gh issue close <number> --comment "..."`

Infer the repository from `git remote -v`; `gh` does this automatically inside the clone.

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.**

## Skill operations

- When a skill says **publish to the issue tracker**, create a GitHub issue.
- When a skill says **fetch the relevant ticket**, read the corresponding GitHub issue.
- GitHub sub-issues represent parent/child tickets.
- GitHub native issue dependencies represent blocking relationships where available.

# Domain Docs

This repository uses a single-context domain-documentation layout.

## Before exploring, read these

- `GLOSSARY.md` at the repository root.
- Relevant ADRs under `docs/adr/`.

If these files do not exist, proceed silently. The domain-modeling skill creates them lazily when terminology or decisions are resolved.

## File structure

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/adr/
└── src/
```

## Use the glossary's vocabulary

Use domain concepts as defined in `GLOSSARY.md`. Do not drift to synonyms the glossary explicitly avoids.

If a needed concept is absent, reconsider whether it reflects project language or note the gap for domain modeling.

## Flag ADR conflicts

Explicitly identify output that contradicts an existing ADR rather than silently overriding it.

## Use case

Lawyers and legal teams use Lexroom to research, draft and review with AI. This exercise is about the review: an AI review of a contract is slow, it sometimes fails, and each successful one counts against the law firm's monthly plan.

Implement the contract review flow of a law firm's workspace, shared by three lawyers, where:

- a lawyer sees the workspace's documents and, for each one, the state of its latest review
- a lawyer requests an AI review of a document and follows it until it completes or fails
- a lawyer reads the result of a completed review: the clauses the AI flagged, each with its severity and explanation

### Rules

- The plan includes 10 reviews per calendar month for the whole workspace. Reviews that fail don't count against it
- A document can have at most one review in progress at a time, whoever requested it
- The AI review is FAKE: it returns the findings listed for that document in `samples/documents.json` one at a time, spread over 5 to 30 seconds. About 1 time in 5 it fails with an error instead of finishing, after having returned some of the findings or none. About 1 time in 10 it is slow, and finishes only after 60 to 120 seconds
- A review still in progress 60 seconds after it was requested has failed permanently. Findings or completion arriving later must not turn it into a completed review or consume the plan. A retry is a new review
- There is no authentication: who is using the app is chosen in the interface, among the three lawyers in `samples/lawyers.json`

### Two people who want different things

Product and the customer have both looked at this flow, and they don't agree.

The product manager:

> "A lawyer must never wait in front of nothing: while a new review runs, keep the previous one on screen. Show each finding as soon as the AI returns it, instead of making people wait for the whole list. And when the plan is used up, take the request anyway and run it when the plan resets, so nobody has to remember to come back."
> 

The senior partner of the firm, our customer:

> "A lawyer must never mistake an old or partial result for the final one: whatever isn't final must be impossible to read as final. Nobody spends one of our ten reviews without knowing it. And nobody should believe a review is on its way when it won't start for three weeks."
> 

The three points, decide on each of them:

- The previous review while a new one runs
- Findings before the review has finished
- Requests beyond the plan

**Note:** Uploading files, parsing documents, authentication, billing and the integration with a real AI model are NOT requirements. One workspace is enough.

{"body":"## Objective

Deliver the contract-review flow described in `docs/assignment.md` as a single Next.js App Router and Hono application. This issue is the parent roadmap for the MVP. Each milestone requires a focused grilling session before implementation-ready sub-issues are created.

Domain language is recorded in `GLOSSARY.md`; the runtime trade-off is recorded in `docs/adr/0001-single-process-review-runtime.md`.

## Agreed product behavior

- A document exposes the latest review attempt and, when relevant, its latest successful review; there is no full history UI.
- Review statuses are limited to `running`, `completed`, and `failed`.
- Findings are shown as they arrive while a review is running, but must be unmistakably non-final.
- A latest successful review remains accessible and clearly separated while a newer attempt is running or after it fails.
- Partial findings from a failed review may remain persisted internally but are hidden as results.
- A completed review with no findings displays **“No issues flagged”** and consumes allowance.
- All review attempts are persisted.
- The workspace receives 10 completed reviews per UTC calendar month. The allowance resets at 00:00 UTC on the first day of each month.
- Starting a review atomically reserves capacity from its request month. Success consumes the reservation; failure releases it. Reviews crossing a month boundary remain attributed to their request month.
- Exhausted allowance and temporarily fully reserved capacity are distinct conditions.
- Over-capacity requests are rejected; reviews are never queued or deferred to another month.
- A confirmation dialog shows quota information accounting for all active reservations.
- At most one review may run for a document. Different documents may be reviewed concurrently when capacity is available.
- The selected lawyer records who requested a review but does not create permissions or private data views.

## Architectural constraints

- Next.js App Router and Hono ship as one deployable application.
- SQLite is authoritative and accessed through Drizzle ORM.
- TanStack Query manages client-side server state.
- The MVP supports one long-lived application process and one local SQLite database. Multi-instance and serverless operation are out of scope.
- Reviews use an in-process asynchronous runner with no recovery or resumption. Interrupted running reviews fail and release reservations.
- Persisted state survives application restarts.
- REST provides authoritative snapshots.
- HTTP polling refreshes workspace snapshots.
- SSE review-change notifications are required for the final MVP; they do not replace REST authority.
- Sample findings are private fake-AI input and must not leak through document/workspace snapshots before emission.
- Authentication, uploads, document parsing, billing, real AI integration, Docker, CI/CD, and deployment strategy are out of scope.

## Milestone 1 — Persistent workspace foundation

### Deliverable

A read-only, persistent workspace populated from the supplied lawyers and documents.

### Scope

- Persistent workspace, lawyer, and document foundation
- Only the minimal review-domain shape needed by workspace snapshots; detailed review schema and lifecycle design are deferred to Milestone 2
- Lawyer selector
- Document list with space for latest-attempt/latest-successful state
- Monthly allowance snapshot
- REST workspace snapshot
- TanStack Query integration and baseline HTTP polling

### Boundary

- No review requests or review execution
- No detailed review lifecycle
- No findings UI
- No SSE

### Completion criteria

- The three sample lawyers and all sample documents are available after initialization.
- Existing persisted state is not reset on application restart.
- A user can select any sample lawyer and browse the shared document list.
- Workspace and allowance snapshots are fetched through REST and refreshed through polling.
- Future fake-AI findings are not exposed by read APIs.

### Milestone grill open questions

- Minimal persistence model and boundary with Milestone 2
- Migration and safe sample-initialization strategy
- Workspace snapshot contract
- Baseline polling behavior

## Milestone 2 — Correct end-to-end review lifecycle

### Deliverable

A lawyer can confirm, request, follow through polling, retry, and read a review with correct quota, concurrency, timeout, and result-safety behavior.

### Scope

- Detailed review, reservation, and finding persistence model
- Confirmation flow with reservation-aware allowance information
- Atomic one-running-review-per-document enforcement
- Atomic reservation, consumption, and release
- Distinct exhausted-allowance and temporarily-reserved outcomes
- Persisted review attempts and emitted findings
- Fake asynchronous runner, including normal, failed, and slow outcomes
- Strict 60-second timeout and rejection of late findings/completion
- Failure and interrupted-process reconciliation
- Latest successful review retained across newer running and failed attempts
- Essential safeguards clearly distinguishing running partial findings, failed attempts, previous successful results, and final completed results
- Polling-based lifecycle freshness
- Automated tests for correctness-critical backend behavior

### Boundary

- No dedicated history UI
- No job recovery or durable queue
- No SSE yet; polling provides milestone-level freshness

### Completion criteria

- Concurrent starts cannot exceed allowance or create two running reviews for one document.
- Reservations are created, consumed, and released atomically and against the correct UTC month.
- Failed reviews do not consume allowance; completed reviews do, including zero-finding reviews.
- Reviews still running at 60 seconds fail permanently; later runner events cannot alter state or quota.
- Interrupted reviews fail without resumption and release their reservations.
- Running findings cannot be mistaken for final results, failed partial findings are hidden, and the latest successful review remains available.
- Core concurrency, quota, month-boundary, failure, timeout-race, late-event, and restart behaviors have automated coverage.

### Milestone grill open questions

- Transaction, constraint, and state-transition design
- Duplicate-submission/idempotency strategy; accidental duplicate submissions are an explicit risk
- Fake-runner timing, randomness, and test control
- Restart detection and reconciliation mechanics
- REST review snapshot shape
- Test tooling and exact coverage

## Milestone 3 — Required SSE updates and MVP hardening

### Deliverable

The final MVP, including required SSE review-change notifications and coherent multi-lawyer behavior.

### Scope

- SSE notifications for running review changes
- Authoritative REST reconciliation after notifications and reconnects
- Coordination between SSE and workspace polling
- Timely streamed-finding presentation
- Multi-lawyer and concurrent-request UX
- Final loading, empty, failure, timeout, reconnect, stale-state, and race-condition handling
- Final verification of partial/failed/previous/final visual separation

### Boundary

- SSE remains a notification mechanism, not an authoritative state store.
- No durable job queue, process recovery, multi-process support, authentication, or complete history UI.

### Completion criteria

- Findings and terminal review changes appear promptly through SSE-triggered reconciliation.
- Disconnecting or missing an event cannot lose persisted state; reconnecting produces the authoritative current snapshot.
- Workspace polling reflects reviews initiated by another selected lawyer/session.
- Required product safeguards remain correct during reconnects, concurrent actions, and stale client state.
- All assignment flows and agreed copy, including **“No issues flagged,”** are complete.

### Milestone grill open questions

- SSE endpoint scope and event protocol
- Subscription lifetime, reconnect, and refetch behavior
- Final workspace polling cadence and SSE/polling coordination
- UI handling of stale confirmations and request races

## Dependencies and sequence

1. **Milestone 1** establishes persistent workspace data and the read path.
2. **Milestone 2** depends on Milestone 1 and adds the correctness-critical write model and a complete polling-based product flow.
3. **Milestone 3** depends on Milestone 2 and completes the required realtime transport and cross-session hardening.

Drizzle/SQLite persistence underpins all milestones. The highest-risk dependency is correct transactional lifecycle behavior in Milestone 2; SSE must consume that authoritative model rather than introduce a second source of truth.

## Principal risks

- SQLite transaction/constraint mistakes could overspend allowance or violate per-document concurrency.
- Network retries or repeated UI submission could create accidental duplicate attempts unless Milestone 2 defines a mitigation.
- In-process execution is lost on restart and requires reliable failure reconciliation.
- Timeout and runner completion may race at the 60-second boundary; terminal transitions must be irreversible.
- SSE disconnects, duplicate notifications, and stale clients must not affect correctness.
- Sample findings could leak before review emission if simulation input and public snapshots are not separated.

## Parent issue workflow

Before work begins on a milestone:

1. Run its focused grilling session.
2. Resolve the milestone's listed open questions without expanding unrelated scope.
3. Publish an implementation-ready milestone specification.
4. Create implementation sub-issues linked to this parent issue.

content.text:
# Lexroom Contract Review

Lexroom supports a shared law-firm workspace in requesting and reading AI-assisted contract reviews.

## Language

**Workspace**:
The shared area containing the firm's lawyers, documents, reviews, and monthly review allowance. The MVP has exactly one workspace.

**Document**:
A contract available in the workspace for review. A document may supersede an earlier version but remains independently reviewable.

**Review**:
One requested AI analysis of one document, attributed to the lawyer who requested it. A review is either `running`, `completed`, or `failed`.
_Avoid_: Job, task, analysis

**Finding**:
A clause-level concern emitted during a review, with a severity and explanation. Findings emitted by a running review are not a completed review result; a completed review with none is presented as “No issues flagged.”
_Avoid_: Issue or warning as names for the domain concept

**Latest successful review**:
The most recent completed review for a document. It remains accessible when a newer review is running or has failed and is clearly separated from that attempt.
_Avoid_: Current review, latest attempt

**Monthly review allowance**:
The workspace-wide limit of ten completed reviews in a UTC calendar month. It resets at 00:00 UTC on the first day of each month, and failed reviews do not consume it.
_Avoid_: Credits, balance

**Reservation**:
A temporary claim on the monthly review allowance held by a running review for the UTC month in which it was requested. It is consumed for that month when the review completes and released when the review fails.
_Avoid_: Charge, queued review

**Exhausted allowance**:
The condition in which all ten reviews for the month have completed, so no review can start until the next month.

**Temporarily reserved capacity**:
The condition in which unconsumed allowance exists but is entirely reserved by running reviews. A review may start after a reservation is released, without waiting for the next month.

# Use a single-process review runtime for the MVP

Lexroom will ship as one Next.js and Hono application backed by authoritative SQLite state. Contract reviews run asynchronously in that application process without recovery or resumption: interrupted reviews fail and release their quota reservations. Review changes are signalled with SSE, authoritative review snapshots are fetched through REST, and workspace snapshots are refreshed with HTTP polling. This deliberately favors MVP simplicity over horizontal scaling, durable job execution, and multi-instance event delivery.

Quota admission atomically reserves capacity from the UTC calendar month in which a review is requested; success consumes that reservation and failure releases it. The MVP rejects requests when allowance is exhausted or temporarily fully reserved and never queues work for a future month.

I’ve reviewed the assignment, samples, glossary, ADR, repository, and roadmap issue #1. The repository is currently a minimal Next.js 16/Hono shell with no persistence implementation.

## Round 1 — M1 boundaries and foundations

❓ **Q1 — Minimal persistence boundary**: Should M1 persist exactly these domain entities?

- One `Workspace`, including its monthly allowance limit of 10
- Three `Lawyer` records belonging to that workspace
- All `Document` records belonging to that workspace
- Document metadata: title, type, pages, upload timestamp, uploader, and optional superseded document
- **No** `Review`, `Reservation`, or `Finding` tables until M2

The workspace snapshot would nevertheless reserve nullable `latestAttempt` and `latestSuccessfulReview` fields so M2 can extend them without redesigning the document representation.

➡️ **Yes.** This gives M1 a genuine persistent foundation without prematurely deciding M2’s correctness-critical review schema.

---

❓ **Q2 — Private fake-AI input**: Should sample findings remain exclusively in the server-side sample fixture and be excluded from the M1 database, seed model, API contracts, and client bundle?

M2 can introduce a private fixture reader when implementing the fake AI. Only public document metadata should be seeded now.

➡️ **Yes.** This creates a structural safeguard against leaking findings before emission rather than relying on response filtering.

---

❓ **Q3 — Initialization policy**: Should database setup use checked-in Drizzle migrations plus an explicit, repeatable initialization command that:

1. applies pending migrations;
2. inserts the singleton workspace and sample lawyers/documents in one transaction;
3. uses stable sample IDs;
4. inserts only missing records and never overwrites or deletes existing persisted state?

Application requests would not silently reseed or reset the database.

➡️ **Yes.** An explicit idempotent setup step is safer and more predictable than initialization hidden inside request handling. Development instructions should make the required command obvious.

---

❓ **Q4 — REST resource shape**: Should M1 expose one aggregate endpoint—`GET /api/workspace`—that returns the complete single-workspace snapshot needed by the page: workspace identity, lawyers, documents, and monthly allowance?

Separate lawyer, document, and allowance endpoints would be deferred until a concrete use case requires them.

➡️ **Yes.** The UI consumes one coherent read model, avoids unnecessary request coordination, and remains consistent with the roadmap’s “workspace snapshot” language.

---

❓ **Q5 — Document version presentation**: Should M1 list every sample document independently, including both versions of the Milan lease, ordered newest upload first?

The API should expose `supersedesDocumentId`, but M1 should not add version grouping, navigation, or hide superseded documents.

➡️ **Yes.** Every `Document` remains independently reviewable, while version-management UI would exceed M1’s scope.

---

❓ **Q6 — Lawyer selection semantics**: Should the lawyer selector be purely client-side context with no authorization effect, persisted in browser `localStorage`, defaulting to the first lawyer only when no valid stored selection exists?

A stale stored ID not present in the latest workspace snapshot would fall back to the first returned lawyer.

➡️ **Yes.** This provides continuity across reloads without pretending that selection is authentication or server-side session state.

---

❓ **Q7 — M1 UI depth**: Should the document list show only useful persisted metadata—title, type, pages, upload date, and uploader—plus explicit empty review placeholders such as “Not reviewed”?

It would contain no disabled “Request review” controls, findings panels, review details, quota confirmation, or speculative M2 interactions.

➡️ **Yes.** M1 should demonstrate the read path and leave clear space for review state without creating non-functional product affordances.

for Q1 - I prefer not to introduce a persisted Workspace entity for the MVP. We have a single fixed workspace with no management functionality, so its identity and monthly limit can remain configuration constants. The workspace would be a derived read model. I do not oppose a Workspace database entity, but its introduction should be justified by a concrete requirement rather than future needs. So no Workspace entity for the MVP

Persist lawyers and documents in M1. Keep review-related snapshot fields nullable and derived rather than stored on documents. Defer Review and Finding persistence to M2.

Otherwise, accept the recommendations proposed for Q2-Q7

The refinements are recorded: review summaries are always derived, polling uses a configurable constant, and tests remain focused.

## Round 3 — Edge cases and operational behavior

❓ **Q15 — Seed conflicts**: If initialization finds a persisted sample ID whose stored public fields differ from the fixture, should setup fail with a clear conflict instead of overwriting it or silently accepting it?

Missing sample records would still be inserted, and unrelated records would remain untouched.

➡️ **Yes.** This preserves persisted state while ensuring “sample data is available” does not silently mean corrupted or divergent fixture data.

---

❓ **Q16 — Snapshot caching**: Should `GET /api/workspace` and its client fetch explicitly disable HTTP/framework caching using `Cache-Control: no-store` and `fetch(..., { cache: "no-store" })`?

TanStack Query would remain the client cache and polling coordinator.

➡️ **Yes.** A cached HTTP response would undermine polling once review state becomes dynamic in M2.

---

❓ **Q17 — Deterministic ordering**: Should the server return:

- lawyers in fixture order;
- documents by `uploadedAt` descending, then ID ascending as a stable tie-breaker?

The UI should preserve server order rather than sorting independently. Future-dated sample timestamps remain valid and are displayed as supplied; they are not checked against the current date.

➡️ **Yes.** This produces predictable snapshots and avoids duplicating ordering logic.

---

❓ **Q18 — Failure contract**: Should API failures use a small consistent JSON shape without introducing a general response-envelope abstraction?

```ts
type ApiError = {
  error: {
    code: string;
    message: string;
  };
};
```

A missing or uninitialized database would return HTTP 500 with a safe message, while detailed database errors remain server-side.

➡️ **Yes.** This gives the client dependable error handling without designing a speculative API framework.

---

❓ **Q19 — Time calculation**: Should the allowance month be calculated from an injectable clock function, defaulting to the current time, and formatted as UTC `YYYY-MM`?

M1 always returns `completed: 0`, `reserved: 0`, and `available: 10`; M2 will replace those constants with derived counts while preserving UTC month semantics.

➡️ **Yes.** A tiny clock boundary makes month-transition behavior deterministic to test without introducing a broader time abstraction.

---

❓ **Q20 — Empty and stale states**: Should the page explicitly support these states even though valid sample initialization normally prevents them?

- No lawyers: show a setup/data error and do not render a selector.
- No documents: show “No documents available.”
- Invalid stored lawyer ID: select the first returned lawyer and repair local storage.
- Failed background refresh: retain existing data and label it as potentially out of date.
- Successful later refresh: clear that notice automatically.

➡️ **Yes.** These are low-cost safeguards around persistence and polling, not additional product features.

---

❓ **Q21 — Contract sharing**: Should the server and client share plain TypeScript snapshot types from a small contract module, with no schema-generation, OpenAPI, RPC client, or runtime-validation dependency in M1?

Database constraints and controlled server serialization provide the trusted boundary for this read-only milestone.

➡️ **Yes.** This keeps the contract explicit while respecting the requirement to avoid abstractions for hypothetical needs.

Agree with Q15–Q21, with two simplifications:

Q17 - Sort lawyers alphabetically and documents by upload date, newest first
Q19 - Keep UTC as the authoritative timezone. Leave the exact clock-testing implementation to the coding phase

content.text:
Accepted. Lawyer ordering will be alphabetical by name; documents newest first. Stable ID tie-breakers can remain an implementation detail. UTC is fixed, while test clock mechanics are left to implementation.

## Round 4 — Product surface and delivery structure

❓ **Q22 — Page composition**: Should `/` be the only M1 product page, organized as:

1. a Lexroom/workspace heading;
2. labeled lawyer selector;
3. monthly allowance summary;
4. document list;
5. per-document public metadata and “Not reviewed” placeholders for both absent review states?

The page should be responsive and accessible, but no design system or reusable component library should be introduced.

➡️ **Yes.** This is the smallest complete interface for the milestone.

---

❓ **Q23 — Display formatting**: Should timestamps be rendered as concise English UTC dates, while API values remain ISO strings?

Document type values may receive lightweight presentation formatting—such as `nda` → “NDA” and `saas` → “SaaS”—without introducing a persisted type taxonomy.

➡️ **Yes.** This keeps the fixture data canonical while making the read-only list understandable.

---

❓ **Q24 — Setup documentation**: Should M1 replace the generated README guidance with the exact local workflow, including:

```bash
npm install
npm run db:setup
npm run dev
```

It should document the default database location, `DATABASE_URL` override, repeatable initialization behavior, and validation commands. Starting the app without setup should produce the agreed safe error state rather than automatically mutating the database.

➡️ **Yes.** Explicit setup is only acceptable if the required workflow is unmistakable.

---

❓ **Q25 — GitHub issue structure after agreement**: Once the specification is confirmed, should it be published as an M1 issue linked to roadmap #1, with three narrowly scoped implementation sub-issues?

1. **SQLite/Drizzle persistence and safe initialization**
2. **Workspace snapshot contract, Hono endpoint, and backend tests**
3. **TanStack Query workspace UI, selection, polling, and UI acceptance**

No M2 review execution, concurrency, quota enforcement, or SSE work would appear in those issues.

➡️ **Yes.** These slices follow real dependencies while keeping each implementation issue independently understandable.

Q22: A single "Not reviewed" status per document is sufficient
Q23: Keep UTC for backend timestamps and quota calculations, but display dates in the user's local timezone
Q24: Accept as proposed
Q25: Once the grilling session is complete, simply inform me that we're ready to finalize the M1 specification

Wait for my explicit instructions before taking any further action

content.text:
---
name: spec
description: "Defines one feature or major change: required behavior, technical design, failure handling, and acceptance checks. Use when consequential decisions must be settled before delivery. The spec is the ticket."
user-invocable: true
argument-hint: "<feature, change, issue, or brief>"
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Spec

Write one implementation-ready specification for one coherent change.
The spec is the ticket: its source may be `docs/<feature-slug>/spec.md`, a GitHub
issue, or another user-supplied document. Update the supplied source; do not
create a duplicate ticket or document. Without a supplied source, use the
Markdown path above. Publish to a tracker only when asked.

## Process

1. Read the request, repository instructions, requirements, architecture, and relevant implementation. Reuse settled decisions and verify claims about current behavior.
2. Define the outcome and scope. Ask about unresolved choices that could change behavior, data, interfaces, security, compatibility, operations, cost, or proof. Leave reversible local mechanics to implementation.
3. Write the spec using the shape below. Explain the change from current behavior; link shared requirements and architecture instead of restating them.
4. Check that a fresh agent could implement it without inventing a consequential decision. Trace success, denial, invalid input, and partial failure where relevant.
5. Stop with the spec ready for review. Do not plan tasks or implement it.

## Spec shape

### Outcome and scope

State the problem, affected user or caller, desired result, constraints, and non-goals.

### Required behavior

Describe inputs, actions, observable results, permissions, business rules, and failure recovery. Reference applicable `REQ-n` IDs. Settle feature-specific product details here.

### Technical design

Explain changed responsibilities, interfaces, data, and execution order. Use concrete types, payloads, state tables, or diagrams when they remove ambiguity.

Cover schema changes, indexes, migrations, transaction boundaries, concurrency, retries, cancellation, security, compatibility, observability, rollout, and rollback only where they affect the change. State important choices, their reasons, and their costs.

Name any required change to system architecture. Do not silently override an accepted rule. Record the proposed architecture change for review before delivery.

### Acceptance and proof

Pair each observable condition and affected architectural rule with a check.

| ID | Done when | How to check |
|---|---|---|
| AC-1 | Concrete result | Command, automated scenario, or manual check |

Preserve existing `AC-n`, `REQ-n`, and `INV-n` references. Never reuse or renumber IDs. Do not invent executable commands for code that does not exist; define the scenario and expected result instead.

### Open decisions

State missing answers, recommended defaults when justified, and whether they block delivery. Write None when settled. Do not hide unknowns behind placeholders.

## Lifecycle

State the decision status and delivery status separately. After delivery, retain the spec as a record of the feature decisions and acceptance checks. Link delivered PRs and proof without claiming unrun checks passed. Record consequential changes made during delivery; do not erase the reasoning. Keep current product and system rules in requirements and architecture.

## Boundaries

One spec may lead to several tasks and pull requests. Use `/plan` when splitting helps delivery. Small, decided fixes can use their task description and checks without a formal spec. Do not require root documents for a local change that does not need them.

## Return

Report the source, main decision and tradeoff, and any blocking question.

# Triage Labels

| Canonical role    | Tracker label      | Meaning                                  |
| ----------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| `needs-triage`    | `needs-triage`     | Maintainer needs to evaluate this issue  |
| `needs-info`      | `needs-info`       | Waiting on reporter for more information |
| `ready-for-agent` | `ready-for-agent`  | Fully specified, ready for an AFK agent  |
| `ready-for-human` | `ready-for-human`  | Requires human implementation            |
| `wontfix`         | `wontfix`          | Will not be actioned                     |

When a skill mentions a canonical triage role, use the corresponding tracker label.

{"body":"## Objective

Deliver the contract-review flow described in `docs/assignment.md` as a single Next.js App Router and Hono application. This issue is the parent roadmap for the MVP. Each milestone requires a focused grilling session before implementation-ready sub-issues are created.

Domain language is recorded in `GLOSSARY.md`; the runtime trade-off is recorded in `docs/adr/0001-single-process-review-runtime.md`.

## Agreed product behavior

- A document exposes the latest review attempt and, when relevant, its latest successful review; there is no full history UI.
- Review statuses are limited to `running`, `completed`, and `failed`.
- Findings are shown as they arrive while a review is running, but must be unmistakably non-final.
- A latest successful review remains accessible and clearly separated while a newer attempt is running or after it fails.
- Partial findings from a failed review may remain persisted internally but are hidden as results.
- A completed review with no findings displays **“No issues flagged”** and consumes allowance.
- All review attempts are persisted.
- The workspace receives 10 completed reviews per UTC calendar month. The allowance resets at 00:00 UTC on the first day of each month.
- Starting a review atomically reserves capacity from its request month. Success consumes the reservation; failure releases it. Reviews crossing a month boundary remain attributed to their request month.
- Exhausted allowance and temporarily fully reserved capacity are distinct conditions.
- Over-capacity requests are rejected; reviews are never queued or deferred to another month.
- A confirmation dialog shows quota information accounting for all active reservations.
- At most one review may run for a document. Different documents may be reviewed concurrently when capacity is available.
- The selected lawyer records who requested a review but does not create permissions or private data views.

## Architectural constraints

- Next.js App Router and Hono ship as one deployable application.
- SQLite is authoritative and accessed through Drizzle ORM.
- TanStack Query manages client-side server state.
- The MVP supports one long-lived application process and one local SQLite database. Multi-instance and serverless operation are out of scope.
- Reviews use an in-process asynchronous runner with no recovery or resumption. Interrupted running reviews fail and release reservations.
- Persisted state survives application restarts.
- REST provides authoritative snapshots.
- HTTP polling refreshes workspace snapshots.
- SSE review-change notifications are required for the final MVP; they do not replace REST authority.
- Sample findings are private fake-AI input and must not leak through document/workspace snapshots before emission.
- Authentication, uploads, document parsing, billing, real AI integration, Docker, CI/CD, and deployment strategy are out of scope.

## Milestone 1 — Persistent workspace foundation

### Deliverable

A read-only, persistent workspace populated from the supplied lawyers and documents.

### Scope

- Persistent workspace, lawyer, and document foundation
- Only the minimal review-domain shape needed by workspace snapshots; detailed review schema and lifecycle design are deferred to Milestone 2
- Lawyer selector
- Document list with space for latest-attempt/latest-successful state
- Monthly allowance snapshot
- REST workspace snapshot
- TanStack Query integration and baseline HTTP polling

### Boundary

- No review requests or review execution
- No detailed review lifecycle
- No findings UI
- No SSE

### Completion criteria

- The three sample lawyers and all sample documents are available after initialization.
- Existing persisted state is not reset on application restart.
- A user can select any sample lawyer and browse the shared document list.
- Workspace and allowance snapshots are fetched through REST and refreshed through polling.
- Future fake-AI findings are not exposed by read APIs.

### Milestone grill open questions

- Minimal persistence model and boundary with Milestone 2
- Migration and safe sample-initialization strategy
- Workspace snapshot contract
- Baseline polling behavior

## Milestone 2 — Correct end-to-end review lifecycle

### Deliverable

A lawyer can confirm, request, follow through polling, retry, and read a review with correct quota, concurrency, timeout, and result-safety behavior.

### Scope

- Detailed review, reservation, and finding persistence model
- Confirmation flow with reservation-aware allowance information
- Atomic one-running-review-per-document enforcement
- Atomic reservation, consumption, and release
- Distinct exhausted-allowance and temporarily-reserved outcomes
- Persisted review attempts and emitted findings
- Fake asynchronous runner, including normal, failed, and slow outcomes
- Strict 60-second timeout and rejection of late findings/completion
- Failure and interrupted-process reconciliation
- Latest successful review retained across newer running and failed attempts
- Essential safeguards clearly distinguishing running partial findings, failed attempts, previous successful results, and final completed results
- Polling-based lifecycle freshness
- Automated tests for correctness-critical backend behavior

### Boundary

- No dedicated history UI
- No job recovery or durable queue
- No SSE yet; polling provides milestone-level freshness

### Completion criteria

- Concurrent starts cannot exceed allowance or create two running reviews for one document.
- Reservations are created, consumed, and released atomically and against the correct UTC month.
- Failed reviews do not consume allowance; completed reviews do, including zero-finding reviews.
- Reviews still running at 60 seconds fail permanently; later runner events cannot alter state or quota.
- Interrupted reviews fail without resumption and release their reservations.
- Running findings cannot be mistaken for final results, failed partial findings are hidden, and the latest successful review remains available.
- Core concurrency, quota, month-boundary, failure, timeout-race, late-event, and restart behaviors have automated coverage.

### Milestone grill open questions

- Transaction, constraint, and state-transition design
- Duplicate-submission/idempotency strategy; accidental duplicate submissions are an explicit risk
- Fake-runner timing, randomness, and test control
- Restart detection and reconciliation mechanics
- REST review snapshot shape
- Test tooling and exact coverage

## Milestone 3 — Required SSE updates and MVP hardening

### Deliverable

The final MVP, including required SSE review-change notifications and coherent multi-lawyer behavior.

### Scope

- SSE notifications for running review changes
- Authoritative REST reconciliation after notifications and reconnects
- Coordination between SSE and workspace polling
- Timely streamed-finding presentation
- Multi-lawyer and concurrent-request UX
- Final loading, empty, failure, timeout, reconnect, stale-state, and race-condition handling
- Final verification of partial/failed/previous/final visual separation

### Boundary

- SSE remains a notification mechanism, not an authoritative state store.
- No durable job queue, process recovery, multi-process support, authentication, or complete history UI.

### Completion criteria

- Findings and terminal review changes appear promptly through SSE-triggered reconciliation.
- Disconnecting or missing an event cannot lose persisted state; reconnecting produces the authoritative current snapshot.
- Workspace polling reflects reviews initiated by another selected lawyer/session.
- Required product safeguards remain correct during reconnects, concurrent actions, and stale client state.
- All assignment flows and agreed copy, including **“No issues flagged,”** are complete.

### Milestone grill open questions

- SSE endpoint scope and event protocol
- Subscription lifetime, reconnect, and refetch behavior
- Final workspace polling cadence and SSE/polling coordination
- UI handling of stale confirmations and request races

## Dependencies and sequence

1. **Milestone 1** establishes persistent workspace data and the read path.
2. **Milestone 2** depends on Milestone 1 and adds the correctness-critical write model and a complete polling-based product flow.
3. **Milestone 3** depends on Milestone 2 and completes the required realtime transport and cross-session hardening.

Drizzle/SQLite persistence underpins all milestones. The highest-risk dependency is correct transactional lifecycle behavior in Milestone 2; SSE must consume that authoritative model rather than introduce a second source of truth.

## Principal risks

- SQLite transaction/constraint mistakes could overspend allowance or violate per-document concurrency.
- Network retries or repeated UI submission could create accidental duplicate attempts unless Milestone 2 defines a mitigation.
- In-process execution is lost on restart and requires reliable failure reconciliation.
- Timeout and runner completion may race at the 60-second boundary; terminal transitions must be irreversible.
- SSE disconnects, duplicate notifications, and stale clients must not affect correctness.
- Sample findings could leak before review emission if simulation input and public snapshots are not separated.

## Parent issue workflow

Before work begins on a milestone:

1. Run its focused grilling session.
2. Resolve the milestone's listed open questions without expanding unrelated scope.
3. Publish an implementation-ready milestone specification.
4. Create implementation sub-issues linked to this parent issue.

set -euo pipefail
issue_url=$(gh issue create \
  --title 'M1 — Persistent Workspace Foundation' \
  --label 'ready-for-agent' \
  --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Part of #1.

## Lifecycle

- **Decision status:** Approved
- **Delivery status:** Not started

## Outcome and scope

Replace the generated starter page and health-only API with the read-only persistent workspace foundation required by Milestone 1 of the [Lexroom MVP roadmap](#1). After explicit initialization, a lawyer can select any supplied lawyer and browse all supplied documents, their absent review status, and the workspace's current monthly review allowance. SQLite is authoritative, Hono exposes one aggregate REST snapshot, and TanStack Query keeps the page refreshed by polling.

This specification follows `docs/assignment.md`, uses the language in `GLOSSARY.md`, and preserves the architecture in `docs/adr/0001-single-process-review-runtime.md`.

### In scope

- Drizzle/SQLite persistence for lawyers and public document metadata
- Checked-in migration and safe, repeatable sample initialization
- One derived workspace snapshot; there is no persisted `Workspace`
- Monthly allowance read model for the current UTC month
- `GET /api/workspace`
- Shared TypeScript contract
- Lawyer selector and document list on `/`
- TanStack Query loading, error, stale-data, and polling behavior
- Focused persistence and API integration tests

### Non-goals

- A `Workspace`, `Review`, `Finding`, or `Reservation` table
- Review requests, execution, retries, concurrency, quota enforcement, or confirmation UI
- Findings UI or exposure of fake-AI findings
- SSE
- Document version grouping or navigation
- Authentication, permissions, uploads, document parsing, billing, or workspace management
- SSR query prefetching/hydration, OpenAPI, schema generation, RPC, a component library, or browser end-to-end infrastructure

## Required behavior

### REQ-1 — Persistent public sample data

`npm run db:setup` must apply pending checked-in migrations and initialize the database with all three lawyers and all 13 documents from `samples/`. IDs from the fixtures remain stable. Only public document fields are persisted.

Initialization must be repeatable and transactional for fixture reconciliation:

- missing sample records are inserted;
- matching existing sample records are left unchanged;
- unrelated persisted records are left unchanged;
- records are never deleted or overwritten; and
- if an existing sample ID has different public data, initialization fails clearly and rolls back its fixture changes.

Application requests must not run migrations, seed, reset, or otherwise repair the database implicitly. Persisted state survives application restarts.

### REQ-2 — Minimal persistence model

M1 persists only lawyers and documents. There is no persisted `Workspace`; the single workspace is an aggregate read model over fixed configuration and persisted data.

Documents retain their uploader and optional superseded-document relationships. M1 does not persist review summary columns on a document. `latestReviewAttempt` and `latestSuccessfulReview` are derived from reviews once the `Review` entity is introduced in M2; both are `null` in M1 and may reference the same review in M2.

### REQ-3 — Authoritative workspace snapshot

`GET /api/workspace` returns HTTP 200 with this logical contract and no response envelope:

```ts
type WorkspaceSnapshot = {
  lawyers: Array<{
    id: string;
    name: string;
    title: string;
  }>;
  documents: Array<{
    id: string;
    title: string;
    type: string;
    pages: number;
    uploadedAt: string; // ISO 8601 UTC
    uploadedByLawyerId: string;
    supersedesDocumentId: string | null;
    latestReviewAttempt: null;
    latestSuccessfulReview: null;
  }>;
  monthlyAllowance: {
    month: string; // current UTC month as YYYY-MM
    limit: number; // 10 in the MVP
    completed: number; // 0 in M1
    reserved: number; // 0 in M1
    available: number; // 10 in M1
  };
};
```

The payload deliberately has no workspace ID or name. Lawyers are ordered alphabetically by name. Documents are ordered by upload timestamp, newest first. Stable tie-breaking is an implementation detail.

Server and client share plain TypeScript contract types. M1 does not add runtime contract tooling.

### REQ-4 — Fake-AI input remains private

The `findings` arrays in `samples/documents.json` are private fake-AI input. Initialization must select an explicit allowlist of public document fields and must not persist findings. Findings must not appear in the database schema, shared client contract, client bundle, workspace response, or rendered page. A private fake-AI fixture reader is deferred to M2.

### REQ-5 — Allowance snapshot

The fixed workspace configuration defines a monthly review allowance limit of 10. The backend uses UTC for timestamps and allowance calculations. Each request derives `month` from the current UTC calendar month.

Because M1 has no reviews or reservations, `completed` and `reserved` are zero and `available` is 10. M2 will derive those values from persisted reviews without changing their meaning. The exact test-clock mechanism is left to implementation.

The page presents a read-only summary equivalent to **“10 of 10 reviews available this month.”** It has no progress bar, reset countdown, confirmation, or review action.

### REQ-6 — Lawyer selection

The page provides an accessible, labeled selector containing every lawyer returned by the snapshot. Selection is client context only: it does not filter data, authorize access, or make a server request.

The selected lawyer ID is stored under a dedicated browser-local key. With no valid stored selection, the first alphabetically ordered lawyer is selected. If a stored ID is absent from a later snapshot, the page falls back to the first lawyer and repairs the stored value. If there are no lawyers, the page shows a setup/data error and does not render the selector.

### REQ-7 — Document presentation

The single product page at `/` displays every returned document in server order. Each item displays its title, human-readable type, page count, upload date, and uploader. Type formatting may special-case familiar acronyms such as NDA and SaaS but does not establish a closed type taxonomy.

Backend timestamps and API values remain ISO 8601 UTC. Upload dates are displayed in the user's local timezone.

Each document shows one **“Not reviewed”** status. The UI does not separately render the two null review fields, expose findings, group document versions, or provide review controls. With no documents, it shows **“No documents available.”**

### REQ-8 — Query and polling behavior

The page fetches `GET /api/workspace` client-side through TanStack Query; M1 does not add server prefetching or hydration.

- The polling interval is a simple configurable code constant with a default of 5 seconds.
- Interval polling runs while the page is visible and pauses in background tabs.
- Regaining window focus triggers a refetch.
- Both the endpoint and client fetch disable HTTP/framework caching. TanStack Query is the client cache and polling coordinator.
- Initial loading shows a loading skeleton.
- Initial failure shows an inline error with a retry action.
- A background refresh failure retains the last successful snapshot and marks it as potentially out of date.
- The stale notice clears after a later successful refresh.

### REQ-9 — Failure responses

API failures use this small JSON shape:

```ts
type ApiError = {
  error: {
    code: string;
    message: string;
  };
};
```

An absent or uninitialized database returns HTTP 500 with a safe client-facing message. Detailed database errors remain server-side. No general response-envelope abstraction is introduced.

## Technical design

### Database and schema

Use the existing `better-sqlite3`, Drizzle ORM, and Drizzle Kit dependencies. `DATABASE_URL` selects the SQLite file when supplied; otherwise use the gitignored local default `data/lexroom.db`. Enable SQLite foreign-key enforcement for every application, setup, and test connection.

Create only these tables:

```text
lawyers
- id: text primary key
- name: non-null, non-empty text
- title: non-null, non-empty text

documents
- id: text primary key
- title: non-null, non-empty text
- type: non-null, non-empty text
- pages: positive integer
- uploaded_at: non-null ISO 8601 timestamp text
- uploaded_by_lawyer_id: non-null foreign key -> lawyers.id
- supersedes_document_id: nullable foreign key -> documents.id
```

Document type remains open text rather than a database enum or closed check-list. Foreign keys use restrictive/default deletion behavior because M1 has no deletion flow. No indexes beyond those required by the schema are necessary for the fixture-sized MVP unless query inspection during implementation demonstrates a concrete need.

Check in generated SQL migrations and the Drizzle metadata required to apply them. Add a TypeScript setup entry point and `npm run db:setup`; using a lightweight TypeScript runner is acceptable. The app never auto-seeds during requests.

### Seed boundary

The setup code may read both sample files server-side, but it must map documents to an explicit public shape before persistence. Do not pass through, spread, serialize, or store fixture objects containing `findings`.

Reconciliation occurs in one SQLite transaction. Lawyers are reconciled before documents so uploader foreign keys are valid. Superseded-document references must also be inserted in a valid order. Any fixture conflict aborts the reconciliation transaction and produces an actionable setup error without changing existing data.

### Snapshot read path

A server-side repository/read-model function queries lawyers and documents and creates the allowance snapshot from fixed configuration. The Hono route serializes that read model directly to the shared contract. Keep query and serialization responsibilities separable enough to test with a temporary database, but do not introduce repository interfaces or dependency frameworks solely for future flexibility.

The endpoint sets `Cache-Control: no-store`. The client also calls `fetch` with `cache: "no-store"` and rejects non-success responses using the shared `ApiError` shape.

### Client composition

Install one TanStack Query provider at the smallest practical shared client boundary. The `/` page renders a focused workspace client view containing the heading, selector, allowance summary, and responsive document list. No design system is required.

Use one workspace query key and preserve server ordering. Store only the selected lawyer ID locally; workspace server data remains owned by TanStack Query. The existing `/api/health` endpoint may remain unchanged.

### Compatibility with M2

M2 adds the review-domain schema and derives both review summaries and allowance counts. It must not add denormalized latest-review columns to `documents`. The M1 response reserves the two review fields so M2 can widen them from `null` to review summaries without restructuring each document. Both fields may identify the same completed review.

This milestone intentionally provides no quota admission, reservation, concurrency, timeout, review execution, or SSE behavior.

### Operations and rollback

Document the local workflow in `README.md`:

```bash
npm install
npm run db:setup
npm run dev
```

Also document the default database path, `DATABASE_URL` override, repeatable initialization semantics, and available validation commands. Starting without setup leaves the database untouched and produces the specified safe UI/API error.

The initial migration is additive to an empty database. There is no destructive automatic rollback. During local development, replacing the database file is permitted only when persisted state is intentionally discarded; normal application restarts and repeated setup preserve it.

## Acceptance and proof

| ID | Done when | How to check |
|---|---|---|
| AC-1 | A fresh database is migrated and contains exactly the three supplied lawyers and 13 supplied documents after setup. | Automated integration scenario against a temporary SQLite file. |
| AC-2 | Repeating setup creates no duplicates and changes no matching or unrelated persisted rows. | Automated integration scenario that runs initialization twice and includes an unrelated row. |
| AC-3 | A conflicting row with a sample ID causes fixture reconciliation to fail without overwriting the row or partially inserting other fixture changes. | Automated transaction/seed conflict scenario. |
| AC-4 | Lawyer, uploader, and supersedes relationships satisfy enabled SQLite foreign keys. | Automated integration assertions plus a foreign-key check on the initialized database. |
| AC-5 | `GET /api/workspace` matches REQ-3, orders lawyers alphabetically and documents newest first, and reports the current UTC month with `10/0/0/10` allowance values. | Hono request test backed by a temporary initialized database, including a UTC month-boundary case. |
| AC-6 | No sample finding field or value is persisted or returned by the workspace endpoint. | Database-schema inspection and response serialization test using the supplied fixtures. |
| AC-7 | Existing initialized data remains after closing and reopening the database/application. | Integration scenario reopening the same temporary SQLite file. |
| AC-8 | A user can select each lawyer, reload, and retain the valid selection; an invalid stored ID falls back to the first lawyer. | Manual browser acceptance check. |
| AC-9 | All documents render in API order with local-time upload dates, uploader metadata, and one “Not reviewed” status each; the two lease versions remain independent rows. | Manual browser acceptance check against initialized sample data. |
| AC-10 | Initial loading, initial failure/retry, empty-lawyer, empty-document, failed-background-refresh, and recovery states match REQ-6 through REQ-9. | Focused component checks where lightweight plus manual browser scenarios; no E2E harness is required. |
| AC-11 | The workspace query polls at the configured interval only while visible, refetches on focus, retains stale data after refresh failure, and bypasses HTTP/framework caches. | Query-level test or browser network inspection covering each behavior. |
| AC-12 | Starting without database setup does not create or seed data and returns a safe API/page error. | Run against a missing/uninitialized temporary database and inspect the response and filesystem state. |
| AC-13 | The documented clean-start workflow succeeds and the repository passes its existing lint and production-build commands. | Follow the README from a clean local database, then run `npm run lint` and `npm run build`. |

Testing must stay lightweight: use Vitest and temporary SQLite databases for correctness-critical persistence and API behavior, with focused component checks only where they add value. Do not introduce browser end-to-end infrastructure in M1.

## Open decisions

None.
EOF
)"
)
printf '%s\n' "$issue_url"
issue_number=${issue_url##*/}
child_id=$(gh api "repos/PavelDobranov/lexroom/issues/${issue_number}" --jq '.id')
gh api --method POST "repos/PavelDobranov/lexroom/issues/1/sub_issues" -f "sub_issue_id=${child_id}" >/dev/null
printf 'linked issue #%s (database id %s) as sub-issue of #1\n' "$issue_number" "$child_id"
gh issue view "$issue_number" --json number,title,url,labels,state --jq '{number,title,url,state,labels:[.labels[].name]}'
